{{short description|American applied mathematician and physicist (1924–2010)}}
{{use mdy dates|cs1-dates=ly|date=June 2020}}
'''Vivian''' "'''Vob'''" '''O'Brien''' (1924{{r|dop}} – December 24, 2010) was an American applied mathematician and physicist whose research included [[fluid dynamics]] and [[visual perception]]. She worked for many years as a researcher at [[Johns Hopkins University]], and is the namesake of the [[Cornsweet illusion|Craik–O'Brien–Cornsweet illusion]].{{r|sun}}

==Education and career==
O'Brien was originally from [[Baltimore]], and was educated at [[Eastern High School (Baltimore)]] and then [[Goucher College]], where she earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics in 1945. Because of [[World War II]], technical jobs were open to women at the time, and she began working in aerodynamics as a [[Computer (job description)|computer]] for the [[Glenn L. Martin Company]]. She became a research assistant in aerodynamics at Johns Hopkins University in 1947, and while doing so earned two master's degrees, in mathematics in 1950 and in engineering aeronautics in 1954.{{r|sun}}

In 1955 she became a principal staff physicist at the Eisenhower Research Center of the [[Applied Physics Laboratory|Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory]], a position she kept for over 30 years until her retirement in 1986. She completed a Ph.D. in fluid mechanics in 1960, becoming the first female employee of the Applied Physics Laboratory with a doctorate.{{r|sun}}

==Research==
O'Brien's research included [[aerodynamics]], [[magnetohydrodynamics]], [[fluid dynamics]], the flow of blood through the human eye, and visual perception. She is the namesake of the [[Cornsweet illusion|Craik–O'Brien–Cornsweet illusion]] in the optical perception of brightness.{{r|dop|sun}}

==Recognition==
O'Brien was named a [[List of American Physical Society Fellows (1972–1997)|Fellow of the American Physical Society]] (APS) in 1976, following a nomination by the APS Division of Fluid Dynamics.{{r|dpd}}
